# Kakacūpama Sutta (MN 21 (PTS MN i 122))

**ID:** MN 21 (PTS MN i 122)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Kakacūpama Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 122
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kakacūpama Sutta* ("The Simile of the Saw") is the twenty-first discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, standing at the beginning of the *Opamma-vagga* ("Decade with Similes", MN 21–30) [Dhammadinna 2014]. Set at Sāvatthī, the discourse is prompted by the monk Moliya Phagguna, who was overly entangled with nuns and reacted with anger whenever they or he were criticized [Buswell & Lopez 2014]. In response to his recalcitrance, the Buddha delivers an extensive sermon on patience, the curbing of anger, and the preservation of goodwill under provocation [Buswell & Lopez 2014].

To illustrate the cultivation of patience and right speech, the sutta presents several vibrant narrative illustrations and similes. It relates the parable of the mistress Videhikā, who enjoyed a reputation for gentleness until her slave-girl Kāḷī tested her patience and was struck on the head with a rolling pin [Sciberras 2014]. The Buddha outlines five manners in which speech may be directed at a person—whether timely or untimely, true or false, gentle or harsh, helpful or harmful, and spoken with benevolence or hatred [Segall 2003]. He exhorts monks to train so that their minds remain unaffected, likening an imperturbable mind to the earth that cannot be dug away, empty space that cannot be painted upon, or the river Ganges that cannot be burned with a torch [Polak 2011]. The sutta culminates in the famous simile of the saw: even if bandits were to sever one's limbs with a two-handled saw, anyone harboring malice toward them would not be fulfilling the Buddha's teaching [Segall 2003].

The discourse was recognized as authoritative within the Pali Canon itself, being explicitly quoted by name as the *Kakacūpamovāda* by Sāriputta in the *Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta* (MN 28) [Kingsbury 2002]. Extant early parallels preserved in Chinese translation include MĀ 193 (where the title corresponds to Moliya Phagguna) and EĀ 50.8 [Buswell & Lopez 2014]. DharmaNexus confirms extensive cross-language alignment with the *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26.193) and *Ekottarika-āgama* (T 125.50.8), while also detecting extensive Pali-internal formulaic reuse across texts such as AN 5, MN 39, AN 4, SN 35, AN 3, and AN 10 [DharmaNexus].
